cards.explanation: The answer is Ziklag, friends. These first helpers come to David there while he's still banished from the presence of Saul, Israel's king (1 Chronicles 12:1). David is banished, and men come to him anyway. I'd call that a good sign.

The answer is that they use both the right and left hands, friends. The text says these archers can use the right hand and the left to sling stones and shoot arrows (1 Chronicles 12:2). That's what sets them apart. I've got one mustache for everything and I STILL drop the cookie box.

The answer is True. The text calls these archers Saul's kinsmen from Benjamin (1 Chronicles 12:2). These are men from Saul's own family line, and they walk over to the banished David. I think that took some nerve.

The answer is spear, friends. These Gadites who defect to David are experts with the shield and spear (1 Chronicles 12:8). That's a pair you can count on: one to block and one to thrust. Same as an oven mitt and a cookie sheet in my bakery, one protects your hand while the other carries the load.

The answer is a hundred, friends. The least of these Gadite commanders was a match for a hundred, and the greatest for a thousand (1 Chronicles 12:14). That's the LEAST of them. I can barely hold my own against one stubborn batch of dough.

The answer is False. These Gadites crossed the Jordan in the first month when it was overflowing all its banks (1 Chronicles 12:15). The river was over its banks, and they crossed it anyway. I get nervous when my timer gets loud.

The answer is whether they came in peace or to betray him, friends. David says to these Benjamites and men from Judah, “If you have come to me in peace to help me, my heart will be united with you…” (1 Chronicles 12:17). He's asking before he opens the door. That's wise, and I wish I'd asked every stranger who came near my cookie jar.

The answer is False. David tells the Benjamites and men from Judah, “…may the God of our fathers see it and judge you.” (1 Chronicles 12:17). He says it as a man whose hands are free of violence. He leaves the judging to God and doesn't promise to strike anyone down himself.

The answer is that they say they are his and are with him, friends. Amasai, chief of the Thirty, says to David, “We are yours, O David! We are with you, O son of Jesse!” (1 Chronicles 12:18). The Spirit came upon him, and his words are plain and definite. I wish I could sound that sure when someone asks if I want another cookie.

The answer is God, friends. Amasai says to David, “Peace, peace to you, and peace to your helpers, for your God helps you.” (1 Chronicles 12:18). The reason for the peace is that God helps David. And Amasai says it with the Spirit upon him.

The answer is True. After Amasai pledges his group to David, the text says David received them and made them leaders of his troops (1 Chronicles 12:18). A moment ago he was asking if they came to betray him. After Amasai's answer, he gives them leadership.

The answer is that they fear he'll switch back to Saul, friends. The Philistine rulers, leaders of a people at war with Saul, send David away and say, “It will cost us our heads if he defects to his master Saul.” (1 Chronicles 12:19). They're worried about their own heads. I think nobody wants to bet their neck on a guy who might change sides.

The answer is the raiders, friends. These chiefs from Manasseh helped David against the raiders, for they were all mighty men of valor and commanders in the army (1 Chronicles 12:21). They defected to him when he went to Ziklag. Good help is a gift.

The answer is the army of God. The text says men came to David day after day to help him, “…until he had a great army, like the army of God.” (1 Chronicles 12:22). It grew day after day, one arrival after another. That's how my own bakery got busy, one hungry baker at a time.

The answer is to turn Saul's kingdom over to David. The text says these armed men came to David at Hebron for that reason (1 Chronicles 12:23). They came armed for battle, and they came for a purpose. A crowd with one purpose is a beautiful thing.

The answer is True. The text says the armed men came to turn Saul's kingdom over to David “…in accordance with the word of the LORD…” (1 Chronicles 12:23). It's not just a crowd with a plan. The writer ties it to what the LORD had said.

The answer is all Israel, friends. The text says these men of war came to Hebron fully determined to make David king over all Israel (1 Chronicles 12:38). They didn't come to crown him over one tribe. They came for the whole nation.
The answer is False. The text says, “…all the rest of the Israelites were of one mind to make David king.” (1 Chronicles 12:38). One mind, friends. There's no argument in that sentence.

The answer is True. The text says the men spent three days at Hebron eating and drinking with David, “…for their relatives had provided for them.” (1 Chronicles 12:39). Their relatives did the providing. That's a lot of supplies for three days.

The answer is joy, friends. After all the soldiers and the supplies at Hebron, the passage ends, “Indeed, there was joy in Israel.” (1 Chronicles 12:40). That's the word the writer lands on. I'd say that's a good place to end.
